title: Using Redis with redux
text: top key/value store aspect Redis, also offers publisher/subscriber model. Publishing redux straightforward; use PUBLISH method: return value number subscribers channel; case zero! SUBSCRIBE method used client deal messages directly (disabled interface prevent ). Instead, use subscribe (lower case) method. takes arguments: channel: name pattern channel/s subscribe (scalar vector). transform: function takes message processes . Messages R lists elements: type, pattern (pattern used), channel value (see Redis docs). transform function can turn anything wants, may side effects printing screen, writing file, etc. terminate: termination criterion. given transformed message (.e., result transform(x)) return TRUE ’re processing messages. Optional, used set n finite number. collect: logical indicating transformed messages collected returned exit. n: maximum number messages collect; n messages collected terminate regardless terminate. pattern: logical indicating channel interpreted pattern. envir: environment evaluate transform terminate. sounds lot complicated really . collect messages "mychannel" channel, stopping 100 messages message reading exactly “goodbye” write: NOTE: need careful - hiredis internally uses blocking read interrupted Ctrl-C started unless message received channels listened ! test , need second process publish channel (’ll wait forever). function publish first 20 values Nile data set. file path_to_publisher (R’s temporary directory) can run : start publisher. Let’s add little debugging information transform function, set subscriber : timestamps printed output show message received (fractional seconds obvious since takes ~1s complete). res object contains values, including “goodbye” end--stream message:
code: r$PUBLISH("mychannel", "hello") ## [1] 0 res <- r$subscribe("mychannel",                    transform = function(x) x$value,                    terminate = function(x) identical(x, "goodbye"),                    n = 100) r <- redux::hiredis() for (i in Nile[1:20]) {   Sys.sleep(.05)   r$PUBLISH("mychannel", i) } r$PUBLISH("mychannel", "goodbye") system2(file.path(R.home("bin"), "Rscript"), path_to_publisher,         wait = FALSE, stdout = FALSE, stderr = FALSE) transform <- function(x) {   message(format(Sys.time(), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%OS3"),           ": got message: ",           x$value)   x$value } res <- r$subscribe("mychannel",                    transform = transform,                    terminate = function(x) identical(x, "goodbye"),                    n = 100) ## 2025-08-01 11:10:27.861: got message: 1120 ## 2025-08-01 11:10:27.921: got message: 1160 ## 2025-08-01 11:10:27.963: got message: 963 ## 2025-08-01 11:10:28.014: got message: 1210 ## 2025-08-01 11:10:28.065: got message: 1160 ## 2025-08-01 11:10:28.116: got message: 1160 ## 2025-08-01 11:10:28.167: got message: 813 ## 2025-08-01 11:10:28.218: got message: 1230 ## 2025-08-01 11:10:28.269: got message: 1370 ## 2025-08-01 11:10:28.320: got message: 1140 ## 2025-08-01 11:10:28.371: got message: 995 ## 2025-08-01 11:10:28.422: got message: 935 ## 2025-08-01 11:10:28.473: got message: 1110 ## 2025-08-01 11:10:28.524: got message: 994 ## 2025-08-01 11:10:28.574: got message: 1020 ## 2025-08-01 11:10:28.624: got message: 960 ## 2025-08-01 11:10:28.675: got message: 1180 ## 2025-08-01 11:10:28.726: got message: 799 ## 2025-08-01 11:10:28.777: got message: 958 ## 2025-08-01 11:10:28.828: got message: 1140 ## 2025-08-01 11:10:28.828: got message: goodbye unlist(res) ##  [1] "1120"    "1160"    "963"     "1210"    "1160"    "1160"    "813" ##  [8] "1230"    "1370"    "1140"    "995"     "935"     "1110"    "994" ## [15] "1020"    "960"     "1180"    "799"     "958"     "1140"    "goodbye"

title: R Bindings to hiredis
text: redux provides interface Redis. Two interfaces provided; low level interface (allowing execution arbitrary Redis commands almost interface) high-level interface API matches several hundred Redis commands. well supporting Redis commands, redux supports: pipelineing: execute one command single Redis roundtrip, can greatly increase performance, especially high-latency connections. socket connections: can connect locally running Redis instance unix socket (Redis configured ) faster communication. flexible serialisation: serialise part Redis command, including keys fields. Binary serialisation supported via object_to_bin / bin_to_object, thin wrappers around serialize / unserialize subscriptions: create simple blocking subscribe client, applying callback function every message received. error handling: Every Redis error becomes R error. redux also provides driver storr, allowing easy exchange R objects computers.

code: # Using a random key so we don't overwrite anything in your database: key <- paste0("redux::", paste(sample(letters, 15), collapse = "")) r <- redux::hiredis() r$HSET(key, "a", "apple") #> [1] 1 r$HSET(key, "b", "banana") #> [1] 1 r$HSET(key, "c", "carrot") #> [1] 1  # Now we have a hash with three elements: r$HGETALL(key) #> [[1]] #> [1] "a" #>  #> [[2]] #> [1] "apple" #>  #> [[3]] #> [1] "b" #>  #> [[4]] #> [1] "banana" #>  #> [[5]] #> [1] "c" #>  #> [[6]] #> [1] "carrot" #>   # Ew, that's not very nice.  This is nicer: redux::from_redis_hash(r, key) #>        a        b        c  #>  "apple" "banana" "carrot"   # If one of the elements was not a string, then that would not # have worked, but you can always leave as a list: redux::from_redis_hash(r, key, f = identity) #> $a #> [1] "apple" #>  #> $b #> [1] "banana" #>  #> $c #> [1] "carrot" #>   # To get just some elements: redux::from_redis_hash(r, key, c("a", "c")) #>        a        c  #>  "apple" "carrot"   # And if some are not present: redux::from_redis_hash(r, key, c("a", "x")) #>       a       x  #> "apple"      NA  redux::from_redis_hash(r, key, c("a", "z"), missing = "zebra") #>       a       z  #> "apple" "zebra"   r$DEL(key) #> [1] 1

Unlike R's *apply functions, callback called side effects return values ignored. pattern Optional pattern use. ... additional arguments passed callback. Note used, pattern must provided (least NULL). count Optional step size (default Redis' default 10) type Type SCAN run.  Options "SCAN" (default), "HSCAN" (scan keys hash), "SSCAN" (scan elements set) "ZSCAN" (scan though elements sorted set).  type "SCAN", key must provided.  HSCAN ZSCAN currently work usefully. key Key use running hash, set sorted set scan.
